\begin{abstract}
Charge-exchange spectroscopy (CES) is the primary measurement of ion temperature
(\Ti) and toroidal rotation (\Vrot) in tokamaks, but photon collection makes it slow
and intermittently missing: on the KSTAR 10\,ms grid studied here (641 discharges),
8.2\% of \Ti{} and 23.9\% of \Vrot{} samples are absent, the two targets go missing
independently, and a further 41.1\% of \Vrot{} rows are instrument holds. The
incumbent way to fill a gap is interpolation of the CES channel itself, which reads
the next measurement and is therefore unavailable online. We show that a strictly
\emph{causal} estimator fills both quantities with lower mean-squared error than that
future-using interpolation, and that what separates the two quantities is what the
fast diagnostics contain. The estimator is a compact two-branch causal LSTM (0.36M
parameters) that reads every grid row of a discharge segment---the always-available
beam-emission spectroscopy, electron-cyclotron-emission imaging and Mirnov coils, plus
the past CES history---supervises the sparse targets through a per-target masked
loss, and routes the \Vrot{} branch away from the fast diagnostics by construction. The protocol
is pre-registered: the test set is never read by model selection, intervals come from
a shot-clustered paired bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples), and every result is reported
in two co-primary populations that treat the 0.53\% of \Ti{} spectral-fit failures
($>$3\,keV) as missing (cut) or keep them (inclusive).

\emph{Ion temperature.} The skill over monotone-cubic PCHIP interpolation is $+0.17$
to $+0.26$ (cut) and $+0.23$ to $+0.32$ (inclusive) with the 95\% interval excluding
zero on all four held-out splits in both populations, $[+0.19, +0.25]$ and
$[+0.19, +0.31]$ in a pre-registered repeated 5-fold replicate that tests every
discharge once, and $+0.08$ to $+0.17$ over a causal Gaussian process with the
interval excluding zero on 8/8 cells; against the offline GP it is $-0.05$ to $+0.11$,
the interval including zero on 7/8. It holds on the covariate distribution of the
genuinely missing rows ($+0.28$ to $+0.44$ over persistence, 8/8 cells) and across a
campaign split ($+0.17$ to $+0.20$ over PCHIP, 4/4 initialisations in both
populations). In the cut population the margin comes from the fast diagnostics:
zeroing them drops the windowed control below PCHIP on 4/4 splits. A pre-registered
four-stage readout (frozen-row equation, trained
equation, full-row Jacobian, corrected form) writes the \Ti{} branch as a
20-parameter physical filter: an observation filter whose gain rises with the gap
since the last measurement ($K_0 = 0.27$--$0.30$ fresh, $K_\infty = 0.48$--$0.53$
after a long gap, transition $s_K = 39$--$47$\,ms) plus a linear response to each fast
channel's deviation from its preceding 100\,ms baseline that is switched off beyond
$\theta = 2.9$--$3.0\sigma$, with $\sum a_{\mathrm{BES}} = +48$ to $+53$ and
$\sum a_{\mathrm{ECEI}} = +44$ to $+50$\,eV per $\sigma$. Trained from scratch under
the identical protocol, that equation keeps 72--78\% of the backbone's PCHIP-relative
skill and 87--90\% of its persistence-relative skill on 4/4 cut splits (registered
bar 0.70) and sits above the earlier increment-form equation by a paired $+0.034$ to
$+0.042$ with intervals above zero on 4/4; the remaining 22--28\% is the network's
nonlinear event handling, which no low-order function of the fast-channel history
reproduces.

In the median, a pre-registered hold-or-jump filter with Student-$t$ noise reaches
0.91--0.92$\times$ persistence on 8/8 split--population cells.

\emph{Rotation.} Under the registered two-level bootstrap over eight new 5-fold
partitions the skill over PCHIP is $[+0.07, +0.70]$ (cut) and $[+0.05, +0.68]$
(inclusive), excluding zero (the fold-level overlap-corrected interval,
$[-0.02, +0.41]$, still spans zero). It is a tail-carried gain from the CES history
alone. The \Vrot{} branch reads no fast channel, and that routing is measured rather
than assumed: the fast channels correlate with $d\Vrot/dt$ at $-0.006$ (BES) and
$-0.003$ (ECEI), against $+0.070$ and $+0.078$ with $d\Ti/dt$. The 100\,Hz Mirnov
values are single raw samples (24 of 24 coils checked), registered features of the
raw 2\,MHz stream change the \Vrot{} skill by $-0.128$ $[-0.544, -0.105]$ (cut; three
test discharges), and the NBI torque is a step input whose slow band carries 0.34\%
of the 10\,ms increment variance. In the median the nowcaster is worse than
persistence; the physics filter's error ratio to persistence is 0.94--1.00 with the
interval including 1 on 3/4 splits, which is the photon floor of a 10\,ms line fit.
The rotation statement is scoped to standard CES at 10\,ms from the core to the
pedestal top.

The aggregate skill is a tail statistic, the offline claim is bounded above by the
offline GP, the value cut is a proxy for fit quality, and everything is one device
and one campaign. We release the pipeline, the pre-registrations and the evaluation artifacts.
\end{abstract}

% =========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ion temperature \Ti{} and toroidal rotation \Vrot{} at the plasma edge govern key
elements of tokamak performance and stability, including pedestal structure, ELM
behavior, and access to high-confinement regimes. The workhorse measurement of both
quantities is charge-exchange spectroscopy (CES)~\citep{Ko2010ChargeExchange},
which infers \Ti{} from Doppler broadening and \Vrot{} from the
Doppler shift of charge-exchange line emission. Because CES must integrate photons
to reach adequate signal-to-noise, it is intrinsically slow, and individual time
points are frequently lost to exposure and signal-quality problems. In the KSTAR
data studied here, even on a uniform 10\,ms grid, 8.2\% of \Ti{} and
23.9\% of \Vrot{} observations are missing---\emph{independently} of each
other---while a further 41.1\% of \Vrot{} rows repeat the previous reading
bit-for-bit (\S\ref{sec:stuck}), so only 35.0\% of the grid carries an independent
\Vrot{} measurement. Empirically in our dataset, the missingness concentrates at
physically interesting moments (low signal-to-noise phases, ELMs, transitions),
i.e.\ it is missing-not-at-random in the sense of
\citet{Little2002StatisticalAnalysis} (MNAR).

Meanwhile, several fast diagnostics observe the same plasma without gaps: BES
measures density-fluctuation structure, ECEI images electron temperature, and
Mirnov coils record magnetic fluctuations. None of them measures \Ti{} or \Vrot{}
directly. The question this paper asks is:

\begin{quote}
\emph{At a 10\,ms timestep where CES is missing, can the simultaneous fast
diagnostics plus the irregular past CES history recover \Ti{} and \Vrot{}
information that temporal interpolation of CES alone cannot?}
\end{quote}

A positive answer would justify a data-driven \emph{virtual sensor}: a model that
fills CES gaps online, without the strong inverse-mapping assumptions required by
hardware alternatives, enabling gap-free pedestal analysis and, ultimately,
real-time use.

\paragraph{A deliberately hard bar.}
The obvious baseline for gap-filling is interpolation of the CES channel itself.
We make the comparison intentionally adverse to the model: the interpolation
baselines (linear, monotone-cubic PCHIP~\citep{fritsch1980}, a local AR
reference, and a Gaussian process) are \emph{offline}---they may use CES neighbours
on \emph{both sides} of the target time, including the future---whereas the model
is strictly causal, seeing only the fast diagnostics up to the target step and the
past CES history. If a causal model beats a future-using interpolant, the fast
diagnostics must carry CES-relevant information that the temporal structure of CES
alone does not contain; and a model that beats future-using interpolation a
fortiori beats every causal baseline. Because the strongest \emph{deployable}
competitor is not persistence but a past-only smoother, we also add a \emph{causal}
GP arm and report the model against it separately.

\paragraph{Claims.}
The paper makes two claims, one per measured quantity; both rest on one evaluation
method, which is described but not claimed.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Ion temperature: a causal nowcast with lower error than acausal
        interpolation, and the equation it computes} (\S\ref{sec:headline},
        \S\ref{sec:model:backbone}, \S\ref{sec:mnar}, \S\ref{sec:campaign}). The
        skill over future-using PCHIP is $+0.17$ to $+0.26$ (cut) on four held-out
        splits and $[+0.19, +0.25]$ in a pre-registered repeated 5-fold replicate,
        excluding zero; on the genuinely missing rows the skill over persistence is $+0.28$
        to $+0.44$ (8/8 cells) and over PCHIP excludes zero on 2/4 cut and 4/4 inclusive
        splits, and across a campaign split it is $+0.17$ to $+0.20$ over PCHIP (4/4). In the cut population the margin comes from BES and ECEI (zeroing them drops
        the windowed control below PCHIP on 4/4 splits); a four-stage pre-registered
        readout
        writes the \Ti{} branch as a 20-parameter physical filter which, trained from
        scratch under the identical protocol, keeps 72--78\% of the backbone's
        PCHIP-relative skill on 4/4 cut splits (registered bar 0.70).
  \item \textbf{Rotation: a lower mean error too, carried by the CES history alone}
        (\S\ref{sec:asym}, \S\ref{sec:physfilter}, \S\ref{sec:headroom}). The
        skill over PCHIP has the registered two-level 95\% interval
        $[+0.07, +0.70]$ (cut) over eight new partitions, excluding zero. The fast
        channels correlate with $d\Vrot/dt$ at $-0.006$ and $-0.003$, against
        $+0.070$ and $+0.078$ with $d\Ti/dt$ (\S\ref{sec:model:physics}); the 15 registered features of the raw 2\,MHz Mirnov stream change the skill by
        $-0.128$ $[-0.544, -0.105]$ (cut, three test discharges); and the median is at the
        10\,ms photon floor: the physics filter's error ratio to persistence is
        0.94--1.00, while the nowcaster's own median row is worse than persistence
        (\S\ref{sec:bulk}). The two quantities differ in what the
        inputs contain, not in estimator capacity: width, model family and context
        beyond 50\,ms are closed axes (\S\ref{sec:ladder}, \S\ref{sec:context}).
\end{enumerate}
\paragraph{How it is measured.} Pre-registration with a scored prediction ledger per
batch, two co-primary populations, a shot-clustered paired bootstrap, the
Nadeau--Bengio overlap-corrected interval and a two-level (training repeat $\times$
discharge) bootstrap (\S\ref{sec:eval}); each piece has a precedent in another field
(\S\ref{sec:related}) and the combination is reported as method, not as a result.
Mean and median are reported from separate estimators, and the uncertainty from a
calibrated Student-$t$ head (\S\ref{sec:bulk}, \S\ref{sec:physfilter},
\S\ref{sec:dist}).

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Profile fitting and gap-filling in fusion diagnostics.}
Gaussian-process regression~\citep{rasmussen2006} is the community-standard tool
for fitting and uncertainty-quantifying fusion profile
data~\citep{chilenski2015,michoski2024} --- applied to KSTAR's own CES \Ti{}
profiles with SVM-based outlier rejection~\citep{Kim2024KineticProfile} --- and
monotone interpolants such as
PCHIP~\citep{fritsch1980,dougherty1989} are preferred over natural cubic
splines~\citep{reinsch1967} near transients because splines exhibit Gibbs-like
ringing at ELM- and sawtooth-like steps~\citep{kvernadze1998}. Irregularly
sampled series admit exact AR-type null models
(IAR/CIAR)~\citep{eyheramendy2018,elorrieta2019}. We use this
ladder---persistence, linear interpolation~\citep{press2007}, PCHIP, local
AR---as pre-registered baselines, with PCHIP as
the headline comparator, and Murphy's MSE skill score~\citep{murphy1988} as the
metric. A persistence baseline has precedent in fusion profile
forecasting---\citet{Abbate2025Combining} report that both machine-learning and
physics-based predictors, extrapolated out of distribution, fall below the
assumption that the profile does not change---and skill scores against a persistence
reference are standard in space-weather forecasting~\citep{Owens2013Persistence}, but
we found no fusion precedent for Murphy's skill against persistence and against
acausal interpolation as the evaluation bar, nor for the term \emph{nowcasting} in
its meteorological sense. Our contribution is orthogonal to this literature: rather than a better
CES-only interpolant, we test whether \emph{other diagnostics} add information
beyond any CES-only method, by benchmarking a causal multimodal model against
future-using interpolation.

\paragraph{Neural diagnostic inference in fusion.}
Neural diagnostic inference has three main lines, and it is instructive to ask
of each: \emph{what happens when the target measurement is absent?} The oldest
line accelerates spectral fitting---NN analysis of JET CX
spectra~\citep{Bishop1993AutomaticAnalysis,Svensson1999AnalysisJet} and fast
\Ti{} estimation from EAST CXRS spectra~\citep{Chai2019FastEstimation}, and the
newest member, on \emph{our} diagnostic: NN-CES, a physics-constrained network
that extracts \Ti{} and rotation from KSTAR CES spectra without beam
modulation~\citep{Lee2026NeuralNetworkbased}. These gain orders of magnitude in
speed over least-squares fits, but by construction they require measured spectra
at the timestep: a missing CES exposure leaves them with no input at all. NN-CES
is the closest prior work, so the distinction fits in one sentence: \emph{NN-CES
reads the measured timesteps better; this work fills the ones that are not
measured.} A second line replaces one inference pipeline with
another diagnostic's: Bayesian-model emulation at
W7-X~\citep{Pavone2019NeuralNetwork}, profile shapes from scalar parameters on
NSTX-U~\citep{Boyer2021PredictionElectron}, and---closest to our targets---\Ti{}
and rotation profiles from an x-ray crystal spectrometer on
EAST~\citep{Lin2024PredictionPlasma}. Lin et al.\ predict exactly our two
quantities, but from another Doppler spectrometer, i.e.\ the same physical
information channel with the same photon-statistics limits; the mapping is
instantaneous and inherits the source diagnostic's availability. A third line
builds end-to-end surrogates for slow reconstruction codes: bolometer
tomography~\citep{Matos2016DeepLearning}, line-integral
diagnostics~\citep{Wang2025PhysicsinformedDeep}, safety-factor
profiles~\citep{Wei2023ReconstructionTokamak}, real-time
equilibria~\citep{Zheng2024RealtimeEquilibrium}, and---on KSTAR itself---NN
Grad--Shafranov solvers~\citep{Joung2020DeepNeural,Joung2023GsdeepnetMastering}
and rapid EPED-parameterized profile
reconstruction~\citep{Jung2026MachineLearningbased} --- the latter consuming CES
as an \emph{input} and explicitly naming rotation as future work. These address analysis
\emph{latency}, not measurement \emph{availability}: they accelerate inversions
of data that exist. Two works sit closer to the availability question.
Actuator-conditioned profile forecasting on
DIII-D~\citep{Abbate2021DatadrivenProfile} is causal and history-driven like our
model, but forecasts from \emph{dense} measured profiles for control, rather
than recovering a sparse channel. RTCAKENN~\citep{Shousha2023MachineLearningbased}
reconstructs kinetic profiles (including impurity temperature and rotation) in
real time and keeps operating when Thomson/CER inputs drop out, via dropout
training; missingness there is a robustness condition handled by zeroing inputs,
whereas in our setting the target's own sparsity is the problem itself, tracked
explicitly through per-target observation flags and irregular-time features.
Across all three lines the common assumption is that the information source is
available when the model runs; recovering a diagnostic at timesteps where
\emph{its own} measurement is missing, from other channels plus its past, falls
outside their scope.

\paragraph{Cross-diagnostic reconstruction and temporal densification (closest prior work).}
A recent family reconstructs one diagnostic from others. GP-based imputation
restores faulty magnetic sensors on KSTAR in
sub-ms~\citep{Joung2018ImputationFaulty}; ML detects and compensates corrupted
sensors~\citep{Mohapatra2019RealtimeSensor}; autoencoders fuse redundant density
diagnostics for resilience~\citep{Kaldas2026DevelopingAutoencoder}; time-series
extrinsic regression fills missing electron-temperature data on
EAST~\citep{Wang2025TimeSeries}, and a CNN--BiGRU--transformer reconstructs missing
effective charge $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ on EAST from exogenous
signals~\citep{Jia2026TimeSeries}---bidirectional, hence acausal, and described by
its authors as offline signal restoration; and FusionMAE performs masked-channel ``virtual
backup diagnosis'' across 88 channels on HL-3~\citep{Yang2026FusionmaeSelfsupervised}.
Closest to our framing, Diag2Diag synthesizes Thomson-scattering $T_e$/$n_e$ at
fluctuation-diagnostic rates from other simultaneous diagnostics on
DIII-D~\citep{Jalalvand2025MultimodalSuperresolution}, and temporal
super-resolution of Thomson profiles from fast radiation diagnostics has been
demonstrated on COMPASS~\citep{Imrek2026TemporalSuperresolution}; a model-based
observer on TCV fills the intervals of low-rate Thomson scattering with high-rate
interferometry in an extended Kalman filter, causally and for electron
density~\citep{Pastore2023ModelBased}; PanoMHD models
multimodal signal dynamics with a causal transformer for
control~\citep{Noh2026PanomhdMultimodal}. Our work differs from this family on
four axes, each verifiable from the cited works' stated scope: (i) \emph{target
channel}---every member reconstructs electron quantities or generic dense
channels (Thomson $T_e$/$n_e$ in \citealp{Jalalvand2025MultimodalSuperresolution}
and \citealp{Imrek2026TemporalSuperresolution}; ECE-type $T_e$ in
\citealp{Wang2025TimeSeries}; arbitrary masked channels in
\citealp{Yang2026FusionmaeSelfsupervised}), and where CER/CES appears at all it
is an \emph{input}~\citep{Jalalvand2025MultimodalSuperresolution}, never the
sparse target; (ii) \emph{causality}---Diag2Diag (a memory-less multilayer perceptron that
maps same-instant inputs to each Thomson time point and is scored against the
measured points with no interpolation or persistence baseline) and the COMPASS
study are simultaneous mappings, and FusionMAE reconstructs within a window,
whereas our model conditions on the target's own irregular past and never reads
the future; (iii) \emph{evaluation bar}---none benchmarks against
\emph{future-using} interpolation of the target channel, which for gap-filling
is the incumbent method to beat, under a pre-registered shot-clustered protocol;
and (iv) \emph{information analysis}---reconstructability is assumed rather than
tested per target, whereas the \Ti$\leftrightarrow$\Vrot{} asymmetry is our
central finding. In sum, this work continues the programme this active family has
established---reconstructing an absent measurement from the diagnostics that are
always on---and extends it in three directions: from electron channels to a
\emph{sparse ion channel}, from simultaneous memory-less mappings to \emph{causal
estimation conditioned on the target's own irregular past}, and from assumed
reconstructability to \emph{per-target tests against pre-registered baselines}.
A literature check (OpenAlex, arXiv, Crossref; 2026-11-09; full-text search
incomplete) found no precedent for the conjunction of these three---causal temporal
gap-filling of sparse CXRS ion measurements---on DIII-D, JET, ASDEX Upgrade, EAST or
KSTAR; we present it as the family's natural next step rather than as a departure
from it, and ``not found'' is not ``does not exist''.

\paragraph{Irregular-time and masked multitask learning.}
Our design borrows standard ingredients from the irregular time-series
literature---observation masks and decay-aware recurrence
(GRU-D~\citep{Che2018RecurrentNeural}), attention over continuous-time
embeddings (mTAN~\citep{Shukla2021MultitimeAttention}), and latent-ODE
dynamics~\citep{Rubanova2019LatentOrdinary}---together with multitask learning
under partial labels~\citep{Caruana1997MultitaskLearning}, late-fusion multimodal
architectures~\citep{Ngiam2011MultimodalDeep,Baltruaitis2018MultimodalMachine},
pre-LayerNorm transformers~\citep{Xiong2020LayerNormalization}, and attention
pooling~\citep{Ilse2018AttentionbasedDeep}. The ``nowcasting'' framing follows
its use in machine-learning weather
prediction~\citep{Shi2015ConvolutionalLstm,Ravuri2021SkilfulPrecipitation}. The
novelty is not any single ingredient but the leakage-hardened combination under a
physics-adverse evaluation protocol.

\paragraph{Methods lineage.}
Each method we lean on is standard in another field, and we cite its source rather
than claim it. Fixing the analysis plan before the data are read follows the
registered-report logic of \citet{Nosek2014RegisteredReports} and its adoption in
machine learning by the NeurIPS pre-registration
workshops~\citep{Bertinetto2021Preregistration}. The overlap correction for repeated
cross-validation is \citet{Nadeau2003Inference}, and the reason a plain
cross-validation interval under-covers is given by \citet{Bates2024CrossValidation}.
Resampling discharges as clusters, with the training repeat as an outer level, is
the hierarchical bootstrap of \citet{Saravanan2020Hierarchical} and
\citet{Ren2010Nonparametric}, with the structure of the Multi-Bootstrap over seeds
and test examples~\citep{Sellam2022MultiBERTs} and of the start-date and
ensemble-member bootstrap for skill scores in decadal
prediction~\citep{Goddard2013Verification}; what we did not find is this combination
(cross-validation repeats $\times$ discharge clusters $\times$ skill ratio). The
skill score is Murphy's~\citep{murphy1988}; proper scoring of the predictive
distribution follows \citet{Gneiting2007StrictlyProper}, and a likelihood-fitted
Student-$t$ predictive distribution scored by the CRPS, with a network that outputs
its parameters, comes from weather-ensemble
post-processing~\citep{Gebetsberger2018Estimation,Rasp2018NeuralNetworks}. Reading a
trained recurrent network through its input--output response rather than its weights
follows \citet{Sussillo2013OpeningBlackBox}, and turning a trained network into a
closed-form equation that is then tested on its own follows
\citet{Cranmer2020DiscoveringSymbolic}; the retention test is the procedure of
\citet{Maheswaranathan2020HowRecurrent} (``recovering greater than 90\% of the RNN's
performance increase over the baseline'') in the non-inferiority form of retaining a
prespecified fraction of an effect~\citep{Rothmann2003Design}, and what we did not
find is the two combined with a threshold committed in advance, or either on a fusion
predictor. That weight magnitude is not importance is the result of optimal brain
damage~\citep{LeCun1990OptimalBrainDamage}, and \citet{Allen1992NeuralNetwork}
reached the same conclusion for a tokamak confinement network in 1992, reading its
response instead of its weights. The Student-$t$ measurement model of the physics
filter is the robust Kalman filtering of \citet{Roth2013StudentT} and
\citet{Agamennoni2012ApproximateInference}. Fusion diagnostic time series have
precedents for a state-space Student-$t$ process solved by Bayesian filtering
(DIII-D; \citealp{Rath2022DataAugmentation}), an interacting-multiple-model estimator
(ASDEX Upgrade ECE; \citealp{vandenBrand2016ModelBased}) and an ensemble Kalman filter
on measured ion and electron temperature (LHD;
\citealp{Morishita2020DataAssimilation}); what we did not find is a hold-or-jump prior
with Student-$t$ noise on charge-exchange time series. In peer-reviewed fusion machine
learning the check found test discharges resampled identically across models,
reported as medians and interquartile ranges~\citep{Keith2024RiskAware}, but no
interval on a paired skill difference clustered by discharge, no pre-registered
analysis plan, no Murphy-form skill against persistence or interpolation and no
response-based readout of a recurrent network---``no precedent found'', not absence:
the check (OpenAlex with full-text search, arXiv, Crossref; 2026-11-10) read mostly
abstracts.

% =========================================================================
\section{Data and problem setup}
\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Dataset}
We use 641 KSTAR discharge (shot) files, shots 30801--32751, selected by the data
provider for hardware consistency and for H-mode ELM-suppression (RMP) phases, and
aligned to a common 10\,ms grid: 247{,}207 rows in total (median 339 per file).
Each row provides BES~\citep{Nam2012AnalysisEdge} (9 channels),
ECEI~\citep{Yun2010DevelopmentKstar} (4 channels), Mirnov coils (2 channels), time,
and the two CES targets \Ti{} and \Vrot{}~\citep{Ko2010ChargeExchange}. On this grid
\Ti{} is missing in 8.2\% of rows and \Vrot{} in 23.9\%, independently
(Fig.~\ref{fig:missing}). Rows are grouped into contiguous segments at time gaps
$\geq 0.5$\,s (a threshold that sits in the valley of a bimodal delta distribution:
only 82 of the $\sim$247k inter-row deltas fall in $(0.1, 0.5)$\,s; within a
segment 99.4\% of steps are 10\,ms): a typical file holds \textbf{one main segment}
(median 301 rows $\approx$ 3.0\,s; 10th--90th percentile 1.3--7.0\,s; 28 files
have two and 20 have none longer than 10 rows) plus a few isolated single rows
(1{,}279 across the set, typically the first row at $t = 0$) separated from it by
gaps of median 6.3\,s. No arm---neither an interpolant nor a model's
input---bridges a gap.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.72\linewidth]{fig_missing}
  \caption{CES missingness structure on the 10\,ms grid. \Ti{} and \Vrot{} go
  missing independently (8.2\% / 23.9\%), motivating per-target masking rather
  than row filtering; counting instrument holds, 65.0\% of the grid carries no
  independent \Vrot{} information.}
  \label{fig:missing}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Two framings of a training example}
\label{sec:framing}
The \emph{windowed} framing (our control, \S\ref{sec:model}) builds a sample at
target index $t$ from the $W$ preceding grid rows: \texttt{bes} $(W,9)$,
\texttt{ecei} $(W,4)$, \texttt{mc} $(W,2)$, \texttt{time\_features} $(W,4)$,
\texttt{ces\_history} $(W,4)$, the normalized target $[\Ti,\Vrot]\in\mathbb{R}^2$,
and a per-target observation mask $m\in\{0,1\}^2$. The four time features---lookback
seconds, inter-row delta seconds, and their $\log(1{+}x)$ transforms---expose the
irregular observation pattern explicitly (the reliability of a past CES value
depends strongly on whether it is 10\,ms or 200\,ms old); the four CES-history
channels are the previous normalized \Ti{}, previous normalized \Vrot{}, and one
observation flag per target. $W{=}2$ throughout (\S\ref{sec:context}).

The \emph{full-grid sequence} framing (our main model) keeps every input-complete
row of a contiguous segment---labelled or not---as context, because the fast
diagnostics have no missing values. Each step carries 22 strictly causal channels:
the 15 z-scored fast channels, $\log(1{+}\Delta t_{\mathrm{prev}})$, and per target
the last observed value carried forward from rows $<t$, $\log(1{+}\text{staleness})$,
and a has-any-past-observation flag. Targets are z-scored with a parallel observed
mask, and the sparsity is handled entirely in the loss. Nothing in either framing
lets a model read the target row's own value.

\subsection{Design principles}
\begin{description}
  \item[No fabricated labels.] We never impute targets to create training rows. In
  the windowed framing a row is kept iff its diagnostic inputs are complete and
  \emph{at least one} CES target is genuinely observed; in the sequence framing
  unlabelled rows contribute context only.
  \item[Per-target masked loss.] The loss is masked per target,
  $\mathcal{L} = \sum_{k\in\{\Ti,\Vrot\}} m_k\,(\hat{y}_k-y_k)^2 / \sum_k m_k$,
  so a row with only one observed target still supervises that target. A
  both-targets-required filter would silently discard $\approx$28\% of labelled
  rows; removing it is a pure data gain.
  \item[Leakage hardening.] (i) \emph{File-level splits}: adjacent rows within a
  shot are strongly autocorrelated, so splits are made at the shot-file level and
  pinned to disk; (ii) \emph{train-file-only normalization}: all $z$-score
  statistics (NaN-aware for the sparse targets) are estimated on training files
  only---the sequence model additionally standardizes each discharge's fast
  diagnostics by that discharge's own mean and variance, which uses no other
  discharge and no target (\S\ref{sec:campaign} shows why this matters);
  (iii) \emph{target-step masking}: the target row's own values and observation
  flags never enter the input.
\end{description}

\subsection{Data-quality audit 1: held (forward-filled) \Vrot{} values}
\label{sec:stuck}
\textbf{54\% of observed \Vrot{} values are instrument holds}: bit-identical
repeats of the previous observation within a contiguous time block (runs up to
1{,}214 rows; 499/641 files affected). These arise because the native \Vrot{}
cadence is slower than the row cadence; they are not independent measurements.
\Vrot{} is recorded to five decimal places with a minimum spacing of
$4\times10^{-5}$ between distinct values, so ``consecutive-equal'' has no
measurable false-positive channel; \Ti{} is unaffected (1 held row in 226{,}991).
Under the confirmed protocol holds are removed \emph{everywhere}---from the
supervision targets, from the history/carried inputs and their observation flags,
from the normalization statistics, and from the interpolation anchors of every
baseline---so no arm can score a forward-fill for free. Every number in this paper
is on genuine measurements only, and hold-free is the protocol rather than a
sensitivity row because holds also contaminate \emph{training} (a forward-filled
staircase teaches a model that copying history is near-optimal).

\subsection{Data-quality audit 2: \Ti{} spectral-fit failures and the two
populations}
\label{sec:spikes}
Observed \Ti{} has p99 $= 2{,}089$\,eV, p99.9 $= 9{,}601$\,eV and a maximum of
14{,}984\,eV: the far tail is not plasma physics but failed spectral fits.
\textbf{1{,}197 rows (0.53\%) exceed 3\,keV}, forming 951 runs in 274 discharges;
85\% of the runs are single rows, only 2\% last five rows or more, and the median
run peak is 13$\times$ the mean of its observed neighbours (IQR 6--26$\times$).
Such rows are unpredictable for every method, and---worse for a fair comparison---a
spike \emph{used as an interpolation anchor} poisons the interpolant at its
neighbours. Two responses are defensible and each is open to a criticism: treating
$>$3\,keV as missing in every arm removes rows no method can predict but invites
``the hard rows were removed'', while keeping them handicaps the offline baseline
by feeding it spiked anchors. We therefore pre-registered \textbf{two co-primary
populations}: \emph{cut} (values $>$3\,keV treated as missing at load time,
identically in supervision, history inputs, normalization statistics and every
baseline's anchors) and \emph{inclusive} (no cut). \textbf{A claim is stated
without qualification only if it holds in both}; a result that holds in one is
reported with its population named. The form is that of non-inferiority trials, where
the full analysis set and the per-protocol set carry equal importance and are
expected to lead to similar conclusions~\citep{CPMP2000Switching}; the two populations
define different estimands~\citep{ICH2019E9R1}, so neither is read as a sensitivity
analysis of the other. The threshold is immaterial across
2.5--4\,keV (\S\ref{sec:cutsens}); the value cut is a physically motivated proxy
(``$>$3\,keV is not a KSTAR ion temperature'') pending CES fit-quality metadata,
and it is one-sided---the same audit finds single-sample \emph{downward} dips
(4{,}965 rows $\leq\tfrac12$ both neighbours) that no value cut touches, and the
cut removes only 19\% of the $\geq 2\times$ upward outliers. \Vrot{} has
fit-failure spikes too (119 rows above 1{,}000\,km/s in 16 shots, 101 of them one
block in a single discharge); the protocol leaves \Vrot{} uncut and every
persistence-anchored \Vrot{} comparison reports the share of squared error those
rows carry.

% =========================================================================
\section{Model}
\label{sec:model}

The main model, \seqv{}, is a \textbf{357{,}570-parameter} causal sequence
nowcaster; the windowed model it replaces is a 201{,}258-parameter late-fusion
network and is retained as the paired control. Before describing either, this
section fixes three things: \emph{what is being estimated}, \emph{why those inputs
are wired to that target}, and \emph{which time scales the model sits on}. None of
the three is measured by the results section; they are what makes those
measurements interpretable, and for the routing they make it a consequence of a
conservation law rather than a modelling preference.

\subsection{The estimand, the loss, and an irreducible floor}
\label{sec:model:target}

At each grid time $t$ the model estimates the normalized target
$y_t=[\Ti,\Vrot]_t$ from the observation history $x_{\le t}$. The loss is a masked
mean squared error over per-target observation masks $m_{t,c}\in\{0,1\}$, plus a
physical penalty discouraging \Ti{} predictions below the normalized zero $z_0$:
%
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{L}
  = \frac{\sum_{t}\sum_{c\in\{\Ti,\Vrot\}} m_{t,c}\,\bigl(\hat y_{t,c}-y_{t,c}\bigr)^2}
         {\sum_{t}\sum_{c} m_{t,c}}
  \;+\; \lambda\,\overline{\mathrm{ReLU}\bigl(z_0-\hat y_{t,\Ti}\bigr)},
  \qquad \lambda = 0.1 .
  \label{eq:loss}
\end{equation}
%
The minimizer of the first term of~\eqref{eq:loss} is the conditional expectation
$\mathbb{E}[y_t\mid x_{\le t}]$, so what this work reports is the mean of the
conditional distribution and not the distribution itself. Uncertainty is handled
separately, by a predictive-distribution head (\S\ref{sec:dist}).

This objective has a floor no estimator can remove. The target is the output of a
photon-integrated spectral fit, so it carries its own measurement noise
$\sigma_\mathrm{meas}$, and even a predictor that recovers the true physical
quantity exactly would score
%
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{RMSE}^2 \;=\; \sigma_\mathrm{meas}^2 \;+\; b^2
  \label{eq:floor}
\end{equation}
%
against it, where $b$ is the physical error. Difference-based estimators applied to
the observed series put $\sigma_\mathrm{meas}$ for \Ti{} in the cut population at
\textbf{46.4--129.9\,eV} (fourth-difference bound 129.9, trimmed at the 95th
percentile 68.7, robust MAD 46.4). The backbone's RMSE of 157.8\,eV is the same
order as that range, and the reason its two ends differ by nearly a factor of three
is what decides the character of the loss: \textbf{46.6\% of the fourth-difference
squared mass (65.6\% for \Vrot{}) sits in the top 1\% of one-step changes.} The
aggregate in~\eqref{eq:loss} is therefore a \emph{tail statistic}, and the later
finding that width and operator family are flat (\S\ref{sec:ladder}) should be read
as a consequence of that fact rather than as an exhaustion of information: in the
bulk the model is still 2.3--3.4$\times$ above the target's own scatter.

$\lambda=0.1$ is inherited from the windowed pipeline rather than derived here, and
the way to turn it into a derivation is to fix a target violation rate and solve for
the multiplier as a constrained optimization. This version instead reports only that
the penalty does not manufacture the result: every arm on the ladder is trained with
the same $\lambda$, and the interpretable rung \bthree{}, which starts at
persistence by construction and therefore almost never activates the penalty, matches
the backbone (\S\ref{sec:ladder}).

\subsection{Two conservation laws fix the input routing}
\label{sec:model:physics}

The \Vrot{} branch of \seqv{} does not see the fast diagnostics. That is not a
modelling preference; it is what reading the two transport equations term by term
returns. Ion energy and toroidal angular momentum obey
%
\begin{align}
  \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Bigl(\tfrac{3}{2}n_i T_i\Bigr) + \nabla\!\cdot\!\mathbf{q}_i
    &= Q_{ei}\,(T_e-T_i) + S_i,
  \label{eq:energy}\\[2pt]
  \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\bigl(n_i m_i \langle R^2\rangle \omega_\varphi\bigr)
    + \nabla\!\cdot\!\Pi_\varphi
    &= T_\mathrm{NBI} + T_\mathrm{NTV} + T_\mathrm{int} + \cdots
  \label{eq:momentum}
\end{align}
%
and both constrain a \emph{rate}, not a level. The question to ask about rotation is
therefore not whether the fast diagnostics correlate with \Vrot{} but whether they
correlate with $d\Vrot/dt$. Checking each term of~\eqref{eq:momentum} against the
channels we hold gives Table~\ref{tab:torque}.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{Term-by-term audit of~\eqref{eq:momentum}. Full 641-shot census, confirmed
  data treatment (spikes cut before held removal), 624 contiguous blocks. $r$ is the
  lag-0 pooled Pearson correlation between a modality's standardized channel mean and
  the target, or its one-step increment.}
  \label{tab:torque}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{llll}
    \toprule
    Term & Physics & In our data? & Disposition \\
    \midrule
    $\partial L/\partial t$ & rotation rate & difference of consecutive observed pairs & measured \\
    $T_\mathrm{NBI}$ & beam torque & no 0-D channel exists & absent (\S\ref{sec:asym}) \\
    $T_\mathrm{NTV}\sim\delta B^2$ & non-axisymmetric braking & Mirnov, decimated to 100\,Hz & closed negative \\
    $\nabla\!\cdot\!\Pi_\varphi$ & turbulent momentum flux & BES sees the density fluctuation & \textbf{measured $\rightarrow$ null} \\
    $T_\mathrm{int}$ & residual stress & needs $\nabla T_i$; we hold a scalar & not reachable \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

$T_\mathrm{NTV}$ is already closed: Mirnov is decimated to 100\,Hz, and amplitude
proxies such as $|\mathrm{MC}|$ and a rolling RMS never helped (\S\ref{sec:asym}).
The one term left was the turbulent momentum flux, reachable in principle because BES
sees the density fluctuation it rides on. The measurement is null:
%
\[
  \underbrace{r\bigl(\mathrm{BES},\,d\Vrot/dt\bigr) = -0.006,\qquad
              r\bigl(\mathrm{ECEI},\,d\Vrot/dt\bigr) = -0.003}_{\text{momentum equation}}
  \qquad\text{versus}\qquad
  \underbrace{+0.070,\qquad +0.078}_{\text{energy equation}\,(d\Ti/dt)}
\]
%
The same asymmetry appears at the level of the quantities themselves
(BES$\rightarrow$\Ti{} $+0.341$, ECEI$\rightarrow$\Ti{} $+0.311$ against \Vrot{}
$+0.027$ and $+0.005$). \emph{Because the same measurement finds a coupling for the
energy equation, the rotation null is not a limitation of the method.} With
$T_\mathrm{NBI}$ absent from the dataset, $T_\mathrm{NTV}$ closed and
$T_\mathrm{int}$ unreachable, the last term is null as well, so no route exists by
which our inputs reach \Vrot{} through~\eqref{eq:momentum}. Splitting the branches at
the encoder is the implementation of that audit, and it is why perturbing all 15 fast
channels leaves the \Vrot{} output bit-identical (\S\ref{sec:asym}). The remaining
lever is acquisition, not modelling (\S\ref{sec:headroom}).

\subsection{The time scales the model sits on}
\label{sec:model:scales}

Three times define this problem. First, the grid spacing is $\Delta t = 10$\,ms, so
the Nyquist frequency is
%
\begin{equation}
  f_\mathrm{Nyq} = \frac{1}{2\,\Delta t} = 50~\mathrm{Hz}.
  \label{eq:nyquist}
\end{equation}
%
The mode rotation Mirnov would have to carry is in the kHz band---EHO harmonics
reported for discharges in this dataset are near 4 and 8\,kHz---and a $dB/dt$ stream
decimated to 100\,Hz without an anti-aliasing filter cannot represent it, by the
sampling theorem. The lag-1 autocorrelation of $-0.009$ against BES's $+0.568$
(\S\ref{sec:asym}) is the \emph{confirmation} of that fact, not its basis.

Second, the time that couples electrons to ions. From the Braginskii electron
collision time $\tau_e = 3.44\times10^{5}\,T_e^{3/2}/(Z\,n_e\ln\Lambda)$ (seconds,
$T_e$ in eV, $n_e$ in cm$^{-3}$), the temperature equilibration time is
%
\begin{equation}
  \tau_\mathrm{eq} \simeq \frac{m_i}{2m_e}\,\tau_e .
  \label{eq:taueq}
\end{equation}
%
For deuterium with $\ln\Lambda=17$ and $Z=1$, $\tau_\mathrm{eq}$ spans 8.3--305\,ms
over $T_e=0.5$--3\,keV and $n_e=2$--$5\times10^{19}$\,m$^{-3}$, and
\textbf{8--59\,ms} in the corner corresponding to our observed \Ti{} median of
593\,eV. The saturation point of contiguous causal context measured in this work is
about 50\,ms, and the two numbers are the same order. This is an order-of-magnitude
consistency statement and nothing more: the plasma parameters in~\eqref{eq:taueq} are
quoted rather than measured here (BES and ECEI are in instrument units, so this work
does not hold $n_e$ and $T_e$ in physical units), and the prefactor carries an
order-unity convention.

Third, the time over which a signal resembles itself. Autocorrelation $1/e$ times
measured across the 641 files agree to within 10\%: \Ti{} 159\,ms, BES 161\,ms, ECEI
147\,ms. \Vrot{} does not: 54\% of its observations are instrument repeats, so
removing held values gives 16\,ms and keeping them gives more than 300\,ms, a factor
of over 19. \textbf{The \Vrot{} relaxation time cannot be measured in this dataset.}
\Ti{} does not suffer this, having one held row in 641 files. The held pathology costs
not only 54\% of the values but the ability to characterize the quantity's own
dynamics, which makes it an acquisition task of its own (\S\ref{sec:headroom}). These autocorrelations are computed without
detrending and are dominated by the discharge envelope, so they are not quoted as
transport times $\tau_E$ or $\tau_\varphi$.

\subsection{Full-grid causal sequence backbone}
\label{sec:model:backbone}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_arch_seq_v2}
  \caption{\seqv{} for one grid row $t$. The 22 input channels (15 fast: BES, ECEI,
  Mirnov, per-shot $z$; $\Delta t$; two history tails of carried value, staleness and
  observed flag) feed two causal LSTM branches. The \Ti{} branch reads all 22 channels
  (2 layers, 160 units; 117{,}760 + 206{,}080 parameters), the \Vrot{} branch reads
  only the seven slow-tail channels (1 layer, 64 units; 18{,}688); each is followed by
  a per-step LayerNorm and a Linear--GELU--Linear head (no activation after the last
  layer). The dashed red path from the fast channels to the \Vrot{} branch does not
  exist by construction; the recurrent state $(h, c)$ passes from $t-1$ to $t$ to
  $t+1$; the loss is the per-target masked MSE on rows with an actual CES measurement
  plus $0.1\,\mathrm{relu}(0_z - \hat T_i)$. 357{,}570 parameters in total.}
  \label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{fig_lstm_cell}
  \caption{One LSTM cell (\Ti{} branch, layer 1, 160 units). The cell state is
  multiplied by the forget gate and incremented by the gated candidate,
  $c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t$, so $\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1} = f_t$
  and the memory length is set by $f$ rather than by compounded Jacobians. Purple:
  values measured on the frozen weights (geometric-mean $f$ 0.465--0.482, memory 1.3
  steps; 0 of 320 units with $\tau > 5$ steps). Red: where the Mirnov input columns
  grow during training (forget-gate rows, 0.58 $\to$ 0.97 against 0.59 $\to$ 0.71 for
  BES).}
  \label{fig:lstmcell}
\end{figure}


\seqv{} runs two independent causal LSTMs over the 22-channel grid sequence of a
segment (\S\ref{sec:framing}; Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}, cell in Fig.~\ref{fig:lstmcell}). The \Ti{} branch (2 layers, 160 units) reads the
full state---fast diagnostics, both targets' carried values, staleness flags and
$\Delta t$---and the \Vrot{} branch (1 layer, 64 units) reads \emph{only the seven
non-fast channels}: $\Delta t$ and the per-target carried value, staleness and
observation flag. That wiring is the implementation of the audit in
\S\ref{sec:model:physics}. Each branch ends in LayerNorm and a small GELU head;
outputs are normalized $[\Ti, \Vrot]$ per row and the loss is~\eqref{eq:loss} applied
over every labelled row of the segment. Two consequences follow from the framing.
First, the model's \emph{reach} into the past is the whole segment rather than a
fixed window---exactly the quantity that separates it from every windowed variant
in \S\ref{sec:gate}. Second, the routing holds at the \emph{encoder}: a shared
recurrent state would carry fast-diagnostic information into the \Vrot{} head no
matter how the head is wired, whereas here perturbing all 15 fast channels leaves
the \Vrot{} output bit-identical (\S\ref{sec:asym}).

\paragraph{What the backbone computes.}
A pre-registered readout of the thirty frozen \seqv{} checkpoints found that weight
magnitude carries no stable information (first-layer column norms are flat across the
fifteen fast channels, the largest weights sit on the least influential input, and
per-channel ranks do not reproduce across splits), whereas the input--output response
does: the \Ti{} output is an exponentially weighted average of the past observed
\Ti{} plus a same-instant response to the fast channels, with a forget-gate memory of
1.3 grid steps. Scored on the frozen TEST rows, an unfitted running mean alone carries
73--82\% (cut) of the backbone's skill over persistence, and a ridge-fitted linear term
in the 15 ten-millisecond increments raises it to 77--85\% (4/4 splits above the
registered 0.75 bar). Trained from scratch as a 20-parameter equation under the
identical protocol with that increment term, $\hat y_t = m_t + \sum_c a_c\,\kappa
\tanh(\Delta x_{c,t}/\kappa) + b_0$ with an observation gain $K(s) = K_\infty + (K_0 -
K_\infty)e^{-s/s_K}$ of the gap $s$ since the previous measurement, the same physical
numbers return on every cut split ($K_0 = 0.30$--$0.31$, $K_\infty = 0.52$--$0.54$,
$s_K = 37$--$40$\,ms, $\sum a_{\mathrm{BES}} = +43$ to $+51$, $\sum a_{\mathrm{ECEI}} =
+39$ to $+46$\,eV per $\sigma$, $\sum a_{\mathrm{MC}} \approx 0$), but the equation keeps
only 50--66\% of the backbone's PCHIP-relative skill (cut), below the registered 0.70 bar,
and a single cross term adds less than $0.001$. The Jacobian of the output on every
frozen TEST row then showed that the form, not a missing state-dependent term, was the
gap: the backbone's fast-channel response is a ${\approx}100$\,ms high-pass (the current
value minus the preceding ten-step mean) whose gain is flat to $2\sigma$ and switched off
beyond $3\sigma$, with no dependence on the recent increments. Re-trained with exactly
that form and the same 20 parameters, $\hat y_t = m_t + \sum_c a_c\,d_{c,t}\,
\sigma\!\big((\theta - |d_{c,t}|)/0.5\sigma\big) + b_0$ with $d_{c,t} = x_{c,t} -
\overline{x}_{c,\,t-10..t-1}$, the equation keeps 72--78\% of the backbone's
PCHIP-relative skill and 87--90\% of its persistence-relative skill on 4/4 cut splits,
sits above the increment-form equation on every split by a paired $+0.034$ to $+0.042$
(CIs above zero), and learns $\theta = 2.9$--$3.0\sigma$, $\sum a_{\mathrm{BES}} = +48$ to $+53$,
$\sum a_{\mathrm{ECEI}} = +44$ to $+50$\,eV per $\sigma$, $K_0 = 0.27$--$0.30$. The
remaining quarter of the PCHIP skill is the network's nonlinear event handling, which no
low-order function of the fast-channel history reproduces. These are measurements of the
model; the headline numbers remain the backbone's.

\subsection{The windowed control: observation-masked attention pooling}
\label{sec:model:window}

The control encodes each modality (BES, ECEI, MC) with its own time-aware 1-D CNN
over the $W{=}2$ window, reads the CES history with a bidirectional GRU (hidden 64)
whose per-timestep outputs are pooled by two independent multi-head additive
attention readouts, one per target, \emph{hard-masked} so that attention mass can
land only on rows where \emph{that} target was genuinely measured---interpolation's
own inductive bias (use only observed samples) written into attention at zero
parameter cost. Its \Ti{} head fuses fast diagnostics, time and history; its
\Vrot{} head fuses history and time only. Everything the two models share---the
data contract, hold-free treatment, per-target masking, the split, the scored
population---is pinned identically, so their comparison is row-for-row paired.

\subsection{The interpretable rung}
\label{sec:model:rung}

\bthree{} (\S\ref{sec:ladder}) keeps \seqv{}'s framing and routing but replaces
each head by an \emph{exact} decomposition, $\hat y = \text{carried value} +
\sum_k w_k z_k + b$, where $z\in[-1,1]^K$ is a tanh latent from a small causal GRU
(64/32 units, $K{=}8$ for \Ti{}, 4 for \Vrot{}) and the readout is
zero-initialized so training starts exactly at persistence. It has 21{,}498
parameters, 6\% of the backbone.

\subsection{The optimization setup, and the state of its justification}
\label{sec:model:optim}

Training uses AdamW ($\eta=10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-4}$), batch 16 segments,
gradient norm clipping at 1.0, \texttt{ReduceLROnPlateau} on validation masked MSE
(patience 2, factor 0.5) and early stopping (patience 6, cap 30 epochs; the
confirmatory runs stopped at 14--25 epochs).

These values are \emph{inherited} from the windowed pipeline rather than derived, and
this work does not hide that. The data and structure axes were all closed by
controlled experiments---window size (\S\ref{sec:context}), held treatment
(\S\ref{sec:stuck}), the two populations (\S\ref{sec:spikes}), complexity and width
(\S\ref{sec:ladder})---but the optimization axis never received one. A single, and
indirect, piece of evidence defends the setting: the \emph{budget-equalization}
condition of the backbone gate trains both models for a fixed 10 epochs with
validation-based checkpoint selection forbidden, and even there the backbone's paired
\Ti{} gain is positive on all four splits ($+0.063$, $+0.033$, $+0.045$, $+0.030$;
\S\ref{sec:gate}). The conclusion is therefore not an artifact of the training
schedule.

The loss axis has since received one controlled experiment (\S\ref{sec:bulk}): a
Huber loss with its scale pinned to the target's 10\,ms reproducibility bound cut the
median error by 8--10\% in the cut population while holding the aggregate skill, and
the backbone's loss stays MSE by the pre-registered rule. That experiment also taught
a coupling: selecting an arm that changes the objective on val MSE picks a nearly
untrained checkpoint (epoch 2--4) in the tail-dominated inclusive population. The
objective and the checkpoint-selection metric are a pair, and when one is changed,
how the other was set is part of the result.

"Why batch 16" now has a measured answer. The gradient noise scale
$B_\mathrm{simple} = \operatorname{tr}\Sigma / \lVert G\rVert^2$ is the batch size at
which a gradient's signal and its noise are comparable, and taking the sampling unit to
be the block---what the training loop actually draws---it can be computed exactly on the
training set rather than estimated. With $g_i$ the gradient of block $i$'s own masked
loss,
%
\begin{equation}
  G = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i g_i,\qquad
  \operatorname{tr}\Sigma = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i \lVert g_i\rVert^2 - \lVert G\rVert^2,\qquad
  B_\mathrm{simple} = \frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{\lVert G\rVert^2}.
  \label{eq:bsimple}
\end{equation}
%
Evaluated over all 452 training blocks at seven points during training, the post-initial
median is \textbf{33.6 blocks} (geometric mean 28.4, range 6.0--61.4). \textbf{Batch 16
sits at about half the measured noise scale.} Below $B_\mathrm{simple}$ batch size and
step count trade roughly linearly, so 16 is neither wasteful nor obviously suboptimal;
doubling it to 32 would roughly halve the step count at the same data efficiency, and
going far above 60 would begin to waste examples.

This is an order-of-magnitude statement. $\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\lVert g_i\rVert^2$ and
$\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$ fall monotonically after the first epoch (10.5 $\rightarrow$ 7.5
and 10.3 $\rightarrow$ 7.3), but $\lVert G\rVert^2$ moves between 0.15 and 1.74, and since
it is computed exactly over all 452 blocks that motion is a real property of where the
Adam trajectory sits at an epoch boundary rather than measurement error. What is stable is
the noise share: after the first epoch \textbf{86--98\% of a single block's gradient energy
is noise}, leaving 2--14\% of signal. The measurement is made with dropout disabled, so as
to capture the noise from sampling examples alone; the training loop's own effective noise
scale is therefore \emph{at least} the figure above, and the figure concerns the
compute-versus-steps trade rather than final skill.

The second measurement, $\mu$P---a parameterization under which the optimal learning rate
does not shift with width---has not been run. Adopting it would make the distinction
between "capacity does not help" and "the learning rate did not match that width"
unnecessary by construction for the width sweep of \S\ref{sec:ladder}.

\paragraph{What the search taught.}
Across two rounds of controlled architecture iterations on the windowed family
(selection on clean validation skill only), attention pooling was the one mechanism
that survived, and capacity scaling, skip topologies and extra extractors never
helped. Under the confirmed protocol the same lesson recurs twice more:
observation-masked causal attention added to \seqv{} is a small, consistently
positive but non-significant gain (\S\ref{sec:gate}), and a five-point width
sweep of \seqv{} is flat (\S\ref{sec:ladder}). The bottleneck in this problem is
information, not capacity, and~\eqref{eq:floor} and Table~\ref{tab:torque} say where
that bottleneck sits for each target.

% =========================================================================
\section{Evaluation methodology}
\label{sec:eval}

\paragraph{Metric.}
All errors are denormalized to physical CES units and computed per target. The
primary score is Murphy's skill~\citep{murphy1988} against the pre-registered
headline baseline,
$\skillp = 1 - \mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{model}}/\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{PCHIP}}$
(positive = model better; 0 = tie). Every arm (model and all baselines) is scored
on the \emph{identical} (file, row) sample set under the same per-target keep
mask, verified bit-identically on the population keys before any paired
comparison. Interpolants exclude the target's own value (no leakage). Neither the
interpolants nor a model's input bridges a segment boundary; where a neighbour
beyond the boundary would be needed the interpolant predicts the persistence value
instead (no population shrinkage; PR2).

\paragraph{Baseline ladder.}
Persistence and a local past-only AR are the causal references of the original
pre-registration; linear, PCHIP and a Gaussian process (exact Matérn-3/2 + white
noise, local nearest-16+16 fit, per-sample marginal-likelihood grid selection,
inheriting the PR2 fallback) read the future. To the causal side we add a
\textbf{causal GP}: the same GP restricted to the 16 past neighbours, with the same
NaN conditions so the scored population does not move. It is decisively the
strongest deployable baseline (seed-42 \Ti{} RMSE 164.3 against persistence's
197.2, cut population), and ``beats every deployable causal method'' is judged
against it, not against persistence.

\paragraph{Three-way split; selection never sees TEST.}
Files are split train/val/test; the test files of every split were reserved
\emph{before} any architecture search and are never read during model selection.
The canonical (seed-42) test set contains $n = 32{,}589$ observed \Ti{} rows across
96 shots and $n = 10{,}463$ genuine \Vrot{} rows across 60 shots in the cut
population ($32{,}721$ / $10{,}461$ inclusive); the four splits (seeds 42, 1, 7,
123) hold 32.6--35.9k \Ti{} rows over 96 shots and 10.5--14.5k \Vrot{} rows over
60--66 shots each. Every number in this paper is read from frozen run directories
by a single collection script, so the text, the tables and the figures cannot
drift apart.

\paragraph{Pre-registration.}
``Pre-registered'' has one meaning in this paper: the hypotheses, decision rules and
numerical predictions of a batch were committed to the project repository before that
batch was run, with the commit recorded; there is no third-party registry.
Rules fixed in writing before the corresponding test numbers were viewed:
\textbf{PR1} the headline comparator is PCHIP (chosen a priori for
monotonicity/no ringing at transients; the full ladder is also reported);
\textbf{PR2} interpolation predicts everywhere the model is scored, with
persistence fallback where no future neighbour exists---and the fallback rate is
reported (0.3--0.4\% of scored \Ti{} rows, but \textbf{40--44\% of scored \Vrot{}
rows}, so ``vs.\ PCHIP'' for \Vrot{} is two-fifths ``vs.\ persistence'');
\textbf{PR3} a minimum test-set floor ($\geq$15 shots, $\geq$3{,}000 observed
\Ti{} samples; met everywhere);
\textbf{PR4} significance means a shot-clustered bootstrap 95\% CI on the skill
excluding zero. To these the confirmed protocol adds: hold-free training and
scoring; $W{=}2$ by the plateau-minimal rule of a 24-run sweep
(\S\ref{sec:context}); a per-file sample cap of 500 in the windowed family; the two
co-primary populations of \S\ref{sec:spikes}; and \emph{model-decision rules
committed before TEST scoring} for the backbone gate, the one attention candidate,
the interpretable rung and the width sweep (\S\ref{sec:gate}). Threshold
sensitivity (2.5/3/4\,keV) is reported.

\paragraph{Shot-clustered paired bootstrap.}
Adjacent CES rows within a discharge are strongly correlated; treating samples as
independent would grossly understate uncertainty. Per-sample paired errors
$\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{model}}-\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{PCHIP}}$ are aggregated by
shot, and whole shots are resampled with replacement (10{,}000 resamples, fixed
seed). The resulting CI reflects genuine shot-to-shot generalization; its cost is
that the effective sample size is the number of shots ($\approx$96 for \Ti{},
60--66 for \Vrot{}), which bounds statistical power throughout. Model-vs-model
comparisons (backbone vs.\ control, rung vs.\ backbone) use the same paired
bootstrap on the same rows.

\paragraph{Replication beyond the four splits.}
A count of passing splits is not a test (4/4 by chance alone is $1/16$), and the
four frozen splits share most of their TRAIN discharges, so an interval over them
is too narrow. Two pre-registered replicates therefore re-ran the backbone as
shot-level repeated 5-fold cross-validation on the 639-discharge universe (TEST
128, VAL 128, TRAIN 383 discharges per fold; every discharge tested once per
repeat; ten repeats, eight of them run after the pooled readout rule was
registered; 100 GPU runs in the headline's
environment). Two readouts were registered before any number. (i) \emph{Fold-level}:
the mean of the fold skills with the Nadeau--Bengio overlap-corrected $t$-interval,
$\bar S \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\sqrt{(1/n + n_{\mathrm{test}}/n_{\mathrm{train}})\,s^{2}}$
\citep{Nadeau2003Inference}, which widens the plain interval by about $2\times$ at
$n_{\mathrm{test}}/n_{\mathrm{train}} = 0.33$ and does not shrink to zero with more
folds \citep{Bates2024CrossValidation}. (ii) \emph{Pooled}: each repeat's five TEST
folds concatenated so that every discharge is scored once in one ratio skill, with
a two-level bootstrap that draws one repeat (training-partition variation) and
then resamples its discharges (shot variation)---a hierarchical bootstrap in the
sense of \citet{Saravanan2020Hierarchical} and \citet{Ren2010Nonparametric} with
the training repeat as the outer level, with the structure of the
Multi-Bootstrap~\citep{Sellam2022MultiBERTs} and of the decadal-prediction skill-score
bootstrap~\citep{Goddard2013Verification}, assembled from standard pieces and not
claimed as new; a cell passes iff the 2.5th percentile exceeds zero. Repeats and
discharges are resampled as crossed factors (every discharge is scored in every
repeat); bootstraps of crossed arrays are not exact, their variance estimate is
biased~\citep{Gallas2009Framework} toward overestimation~\citep{Owen2007Pigeonhole},
so the interval is conservative. For \Ti{} the two agree to the second decimal. For
\Vrot{}, whose $\approx$80-discharge folds are set by a few heavy-error discharges
(fold-to-fold s.d.\ 0.18), the fold-level interval spans zero while the pooled one
does not; the registration named the pooled two-level readout, computed on the
eight repeats run after the rule was written, as the deciding one for the
replicate, and Table~\ref{tab:replicate} reports both.

\paragraph{The MNAR problem, and what we do about it.}
Truly missing points have no ground truth, so skill is measured by masking
\emph{observed} points. Because CES missingness is MNAR (drop-out at low S/N, ELMs,
transitions), observed-point skill is an optimistic estimate of performance at
genuinely missing points. \S\ref{sec:mnar} reweights the scored points onto the
covariate distribution of the \emph{actually missing} ones and reports how much of
the skill survives, together with what fraction of the missing population is in
the analysis' domain at all.

% =========================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{The nowcaster has the lowest RMSE of every causal baseline}
Table~\ref{tab:ladder} shows the physical-unit RMSE ladder on the canonical test
split. \seqv{} has the lowest RMSE for both targets among all methods that do not
read the future, 4\% (\Ti) and 18\% (\Vrot) below the causal GP---the strongest
deployable arm---and below the future-using interpolants; the offline GP, which
averages noisy anchors rather than passing through them, is the one arm with a lower
\Ti{} RMSE (153.8 vs.\ 157.8; paired skill $-0.05$ to $+0.11$ with the CI including
zero on 7/8 cells, \S\ref{sec:headline}). This is the most robust result in the
paper: for any online setting, where future CES is by definition unavailable, the
sequence nowcaster has the lowest error.

\subsection{The full-grid framing against the windowed control: the backbone gate}
\label{sec:gate}
The sequence framing was adopted under a pre-registered four-condition gate, scored
once in the cut population on a $4\times 4$ grid of split seed $\times$ initialisation
seed, each run paired row-for-row against its split's $W{=}2$ windowed control. The
paired \Ti{} skill is positive on \textbf{16/16 runs} (CI above zero on 13/16), with
pooled mean $\mathbf{+0.081}$ and run-cluster 95\% CI $[+0.067, +0.096]$, excluding
zero; a budget-equalized arm (fixed 10 epochs, final weights, no validation selection)
keeps the sign on 4/4 splits ($+0.063$, $+0.033$, $+0.045$, $+0.030$), and no run has
a significant \Vrot{} deficit, so all four conditions hold. What the framing buys is
reach: the windowed control's skill over the causal GP is $+0.041$ with the CI
including zero on 3/4 splits (cut), and the backbone's is $+0.08$ to $+0.17$ with CIs
above zero on 4/4 in both populations. Every model decision was taken on validation
data or under a rule committed in writing before the corresponding TEST scoring, with
TEST scored once per decision. Under the same rule the one architectural candidate
explored afterwards---observation-masked causal attention over each target's own past
observation steps, added to \seqv{}---has a paired \Ti{} skill against the backbone
of $+0.009$, $+0.013$, $+0.033$, $+0.020$, with the CI above zero on 1/4 splits
against a pre-committed bar of $\geq 3/4$, so it was not promoted.

\subsection{Where the skill lives: gap regime}
\label{sec:gap}
Stratifying by $\Delta t$, the time since the last observed CES value, $\geq$96\% of
scored targets lie in the adjacent regime ($\Delta t \leq 15$\,ms); per split the
wide bins hold only hundreds of samples, so we \emph{pool the four test splits} and
cluster the bootstrap on the physical discharge (Table~\ref{tab:gap}). As
$\Delta t$ grows PCHIP's task gets \emph{easier}---it interpolates between two real
observations that straddle the gap---while ours gets harder, so this is the
regime where a causal method is least expected to win.

\subsection{How much of this survives at the points that are actually missing?}
\label{sec:mnar}

Everything above is measured on CES points that happen to be \emph{observed}. We
can never measure error where there is no ground truth---but we can measure how
skill varies over covariates that are computable at observed \emph{and} missing
rows, and reweight. Two covariates carry the mechanism: $\Delta t$ since the last
genuine observation, binned at 15/25/45\,ms, and the input-only local-activity
flag of \S\ref{sec:peak}, which is defined at a missing row because it is computed
from a neighbour set that excludes the row itself. We post-stratify on
$\Delta t \times$ activity, drop any stratum with fewer than 30 scored samples,
and report the surviving coverage next to every estimate; the weight grid is
population-consistent (the cut is applied to it too). The assumption---that within
a stratum missing and observed rows are exchangeable---is stated, not assumed away.

\paragraph{First, a scope result.} The analysis' domain is ``a genuine observation
of that target within two rows'', the $W{=}2$ criterion. Of the genuinely missing
\Ti{} rows, \textbf{54--68\% are in-domain} per split; of the genuinely missing
\Vrot{} rows, \textbf{only 4--6\%} are, because \Vrot{} gaps are long blocks
(coverage of surviving strata 0.99 for \Ti{}, 0.73--0.76 for \Vrot{}). The
reweighted \Vrot{} row therefore answers a question about one-twentieth of the
missing mass and we draw nothing from it.

      & 42  & $+0.225$ & $\mathbf{+0.140}$ $[+0.033, +0.250]$ & $+0.423$ & $\mathbf{+0.443}$ $[+0.141, +0.623]$ \\
      & 1   & $+0.238$ & $\mathbf{+0.217}$ $[+0.086, +0.319]$ & $+0.436$ & $\mathbf{+0.383}$ $[+0.273, +0.536]$ \\
      & 7   & $+0.292$ & $\mathbf{+0.167}$ $[+0.067, +0.265]$ & $+0.406$ & $\mathbf{+0.283}$ $[+0.172, +0.380]$ \\
      & 123 & $+0.316$ & $\mathbf{+0.221}$ $[+0.050, +0.320]$ & $+0.459$ & $\mathbf{+0.337}$ $[+0.164, +0.455]$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Second, the two comparisons come apart---and the split is the useful
thing.} Against \textbf{persistence---the baseline an online system actually
runs---the \Ti{} skill survives reweighting on all four splits in both
populations} ($+0.28$ to $+0.44$, every CI excluding zero); the MNAR correction
costs at most $0.12$ of skill and on some splits nothing. Against
\textbf{future-using PCHIP} the reweighted point estimates stay at $+0.14$ to
$+0.28$ but the wide fixed-weight CIs pass through zero on two cut-population
splits (2/4 significant; 4/4 inclusive). Missing points sit at larger
$\Delta t$, which is where a two-sided anchor helps most and where the reweighting
bootstrap is thinnest. The claim the evidence supports at the points that matter
is therefore: \emph{at genuinely missing, in-domain timesteps the nowcaster is
significantly better than any causal CES-only method in both populations, and
better than offline interpolation with a population-conditional significance
(2/4 cut, 4/4 inclusive)}. The windowed control behaves the same way (2/4 and
4/4 vs.\ PCHIP; 4/4 vs.\ persistence).

\subsection{Does it survive a campaign shift?}
\label{sec:campaign}

The second thing deployment does that a random split does not is move forward in
time. We order all 641 discharges by shot number (30801--32751) and cut strictly in
time: \textbf{train 416 shots [30801, 31991], val 128 [32002, 32310], test 97
[32312, 32751]}, no test shot preceding any train shot. Everything else is pinned
to the headline protocol, so the only changed variable is the split rule; the
split is fixed, so the four runs vary the \emph{initialisation} seed only, and we
say so rather than presenting them as four splits. Three arms per population:
the windowed control as trained for the headline (train-file-only
normalization), the same control with per-shot standardization of the fast
diagnostics (cut population), and \seqv{} (Table~\ref{tab:campaign}).

  \label{tab:campaign}
  \small
  \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%

      & control, per-shot std.\ (ON) & $\mathbf{+0.103}$ / $\mathbf{+0.107}$ / $\mathbf{+0.094}$ / $\mathbf{+0.107}$ & 4/4 & --- & --- \\
